reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: In children deficiency causes rickets with bowing of the legs, widened wrists, a rachitic rosary, and delayed growth; in adults it causes osteomalacia with bone pain and proximal myopathy
It is highly prevalent across India despite abundant sunshine, owing to skin pigmentation, covering clothing, indoor lifestyles, air pollution, and low dietary intake
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the best marker of body stores; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is not a reliable indicator of deficiency
Biochemistry classically shows low or low-normal calcium and phosphate with a raised alkaline phosphatase and secondary hyperparathyroidism
Risk groups include exclusively breastfed infants without supplementation, older housebound adults, and people with malabsorption or chronic kidney or liver disease
Proximal muscle weakness and increased fall and fracture risk are important, sometimes overlooked, consequences
Correction of deficiency together with adequate calcium intake improves bone mineralisation and muscle function
reference.pathophysiology: Vitamin D is synthesised in skin under ultraviolet B exposure and obtained in smaller amounts from diet, then hydroxylated in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D and in the kidney to the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Its main role is to maintain calcium and phosphate homeostasis by enhancing intestinal absorption and supporting bone mineralisation. Deficiency reduces calcium and phosphate absorption, provoking secondary hyperparathyroidism that mobilises calcium from bone and increases phosphate loss. The resulting failure to mineralise osteoid produces soft bone: rickets at the growth plates of children and osteomalacia in adults.
additionalDifferentials: Renal osteodystrophy in chronic kidney disease
Hypophosphataemic rickets and other inherited defects
Malignancy or other cause of bone pain
Inflammatory myopathy for the muscle weakness
additionalInvestigations: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D as the primary measure of status
Calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone
Renal and liver function, given their role in vitamin D activation
Radiographs showing looser zones (pseudofractures) or rachitic growth-plate changes
Assessment for malabsorption when deficiency is severe or refractory
redFlags: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, laryngospasm, or seizures
Severe deficiency in an infant with hypocalcaemic seizures or cardiomyopathy
Refractory deficiency suggesting malabsorption or renal or hepatic disease
reference.prognosis: With adequate replacement and calcium intake, bone mineralisation and muscle strength recover and childhood rickets heals, though severe or prolonged rickets may leave residual skeletal deformity.
pitfalls: Measuring 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D instead of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to assess status
Treating vitamin D without ensuring adequate calcium intake
Overlooking deficiency as a cause of proximal myopathy and falls in older adults
Missing severe hypocalcaemia before starting treatment
